passage_text: Researchers at the National Institute of Sleep Studies investigated how acute sleep deprivation affects cognitive performance. Twenty healthy adults (10 male, 10 female) were randomly assigned to either a sleep-deprived group (n = 10) or a well-rested control group (n = 10). All participants completed a standardized neuropsychological battery after 8 hours of sleep (control) or after 24 hours of wakefulness (deprived). The battery included a simple reaction time task, a working memory task (n-back), and a verbal recall test. The researchers recorded reaction times (ms), working memory scores (percentage correct), and verbal recall scores (number of words recalled). Data for five representative participants (three controls and two sleep-deprived) are shown in Table 1. The study aimed to determine whether sleep deprivation leads to measurable declines in processing speed, memory accuracy, and recall ability, and to assess whether these effects differ by sex or age.
table_data:
Table 1: Cognitive Performance by Sleep Condition

| Participant | Condition | Hours Slept | Reaction Time (ms) | Working Memory % | Verbal Recall |
|-------------|-----------|-------------|--------------------|------------------|---------------|
| 1           | Control   | 8           | 215                | 92               | 14            |
| 2           | Control   | 8           | 198                | 88               | 13            |
| 3           | Deprived  | 0           | 312                | 74               | 9             |
| 4           | Deprived  | 0           | 298                | 78               | 10            |
| 5           | Control   | 8           | 210                | 90               | 15            |
stem: Which participant exhibited the fastest reaction time?
explanation: Participant 2 had the lowest reaction time (198 ms), which is faster than all other participants listed in the table.
trap: Picking Participant 1 because 215 ms is the first control value listed, overlooking that Participant 2's 198 ms is the lowest reaction time in the table.

stem: Which of the following best describes an appropriate control condition for this study?

options.A: Participants who are given caffeine before testing
options.B: Participants who are allowed to nap for 30 minutes during the experiment
options.C: Participants who sleep normally (8 hours) the night before testing
options.D: Participants who are exposed to bright light for 2 hours before testing

explanation: The control group in the study consisted of participants who received 8 hours of normal sleep, providing a baseline against which the effects of sleep deprivation can be measured.
trap: Choosing caffeine or bright light exposure as controls may introduce additional variables that affect cognition, confounding the results.

stem: What is the average reaction time (in ms) of the two sleep-deprived participants shown in Table 1?
explanation: Correct: Participants 3 and 4 had reaction times of 312 and 298 ms, so the mean is (312 + 298) / 2 = 305 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) 231 ms is not the mean of any combination of the deprived values. C) 268 ms does not match the mean of the two deprived participants. D) 215 ms is Participant 1's control reaction time.
trap: Averaging in a control participant or using only one deprived value (312 ms) gives the wrong mean.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by Table 1?

options.A: The two sleep-deprived participants shown had slower reaction times than all three controls shown.
options.B: The two sleep-deprived participants shown had lower working memory percentages than all three controls shown.
options.C: The two sleep-deprived participants shown recalled fewer words than all three controls shown.
options.D: Sleep deprivation impaired performance more in female participants than in male participants.

explanation: Correct: Table 1 does not list the sex of any participant, so no sex difference can be inferred. Why the others are wrong: A) Deprived RTs were 312 and 298 ms versus 215, 198 and 210 ms for controls, so this is supported. B) Deprived scores were 74 and 78% versus 92, 88 and 90%, so this is supported. C) Deprived participants recalled 9 and 10 words versus 14, 13 and 15, so this is supported.
trap: Assuming the passage's stated aim of testing sex differences means the table contains sex-specific results.

stem: Which feature of the study design best supports attributing the performance differences to sleep condition rather than to pre-existing differences between participants?

options.A: Random assignment of participants to the sleep-deprived or control group
options.B: Reporting the hours slept for each participant in Table 1

explanation: Correct: random assignment makes the two groups comparable at the outset so that differences are attributable to sleep condition. Why the others are wrong: B) Recording hours slept describes the manipulation but does not balance participant characteristics. C) The unit of measurement has no bearing on causal attribution. D) Using several tests broadens the outcomes measured but does not equate the groups.
trap: Choosing the hours-slept column because it documents the manipulation, although recording hours slept does not equate the groups' pre-existing traits; only random assignment does.
